extracted.intended_audience: general readers of humorous travel literature; writers studying comic travelogue techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit criteria for composing or evaluating first‑person humorous travel writing (vivid scene description, satirical commentary, comic voice, and digression). Focus is on 19th‑century-style travelogue satire but applicable broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aphorism then subversion
rubrics_metrics.description: "See Naples and die." Well, I do not know that one would necessarily die after merely seeing it, but to attempt to live there might turn out a little differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with a familiar, pithy aphorism to hook the reader, then undercut or qualify it for comic effect. Example on page: state an epigrammatic proverb and immediately deflate it with a literal or contrary observation. Anti-pattern: leaving the aphorism unexamined (no payoff) or treating it reverently so the reader expects seriousness instead of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve romantic distance (vantage matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is from the Hermitage, there on the side of Vesuvius, that one should 'see Naples and die.' But do not go within the walls and look at it in detail. That takes away some of the romance of the thing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise choice of viewpoint: describing a scene from a particular distance can preserve idealized romance; close inspection invites comic or unromantic detail. Use as a writerly guideline: select vantage deliberately to control tone. Anti-pattern: insisting on 'authentic detail' that destroys the intended mood without comedic intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggerated numeric hyperbole
rubrics_metrics.description: "I honestly believe a good majority of them are a hundred feet high! And the solid brick walls are seven feet through. You go up nine flights of stairs before you get to the 'first' floor."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise-sounding numeric exaggeration to produce absurdity — the specificity makes the hyperbole funnier. Example: absurd building heights/ wall thickness. Avoid arbitrary vagueness that dilutes the comic effect; don't rely on unbelievable figures without a deadpan delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juxtaposition of opulence and squalor
rubrics_metrics.description: "The contrasts between opulence and poverty, and magnificence and misery, are more frequent and more striking in Naples... Naked boys of nine years and the fancy-dressed children of luxury... jackass-carts and state-carriages... Dukes and bankers... turn out, also, and so the furious procession goes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place extreme opposites side by side to highlight social absurdities and create comic tension. Use parallel listing and contrast. Anti-pattern: moralizing or sentimentalizing the contrast when the intention is satirical observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid perspective and concrete simile
rubrics_metrics.description: "The perspective of one of these narrow cracks of streets... with its rows of tall houses stretching away till they come together in the distance like railway tracks..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ strong visual metaphors and concrete similes (railway tracks, martin-boxes) to create an immediately comprehensible and funny image. Choose comparisons that are slightly incongruous for comedic effect. Avoid abstract or over-worn similes that flatten the image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parenthetical comic asides
rubrics_metrics.description: "Princes (there are more Princes than policemen in Naples--the city is infested with them)--Princes who live up seven flights of stairs and don't own any principalities..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parenthetical remarks or dashes to add a quick ironic observation or punchline inside a larger sentence. These asides can heighten voice and deliver small jokes without breaking the narrative flow. Anti-pattern: overuse that fragments the prose or makes the voice seem scattered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical modern-parallel digression
rubrics_metrics.description: "...the pavements were not repaired!--how ruts five and even ten inches deep were worn into the thick flagstones by the chariot-wheels of generations of swindled tax-payers? And do I not know by these signs that Street Commissioners of Pompeii never attended to their business..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make humorous contemporary parallels (bureaucracy, civic neglect) when describing historical or foreign scenes to expose universal follies. A well-placed digression reframes the subject and delivers satire. Avoid tired clichés or forced parallels that feel shoehorned in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mock-document / parody of scholarship
rubrics_metrics.description: Invented encyclopedia entry: a ridiculous future account of 'URIAH S. (or Z.) GRAUNT' with garbled dates and faux‑scholarship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody authoritative forms (encyclopedia, footnotes) to lampoon pretensions of history and fame. Fake scholarly asides can deepen satire by imitating learned language while subverting it. Anti-pattern: imitating the form without a clear satirical target, which reads as confusion rather than wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irony and reversal for a punchline
rubrics_metrics.description: "Let us remember that he was a soldier--not a policeman --and so, praise him. Being a soldier, he staid,--because the warrior instinct forbade him to fly. Had he been a policeman he would have staid, also--because he would have been asleep."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build expectation and then reverse it with an ironic twist; couched as a sober moral, the reversal becomes the joke. Use sparing, pointed reversals for maximal effect. Anti-pattern: telegraphed reversals or ones that insult without wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic literalism / character misunderstanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue: the Oracle confuses Scylla and Charybdis with Sodom and Gomorrah: 'It ain't mentioned in the Bible!--this place ain't--well now, what place is this, since you know so much about it?' 'Why it's Scylla and Charybdis.' 'Scylla and Cha--confound it, I thought it was Sodom and Gomorrah!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use characters' ignorance or literal misreading for comic effect; short, colloquial dialogue highlights the mismatch between learned references and everyday understanding. Avoid mean-spirited portrayal; aim for affectionate mockery of pretension or confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadpan dangerous levity (normalize the absurd)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Some of the boys thrust long slips of paper down into holes and set them on fire, and so achieved the glory of lighting their cigars by the flames of Vesuvius, and others cooked eggs over fissures in the rocks and were happy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe risky or spectacular phenomena in a calm, mundane tone (deadpan) to produce humor by contrast. Treating the extraordinary as quotidian is an effective comic device. Anti-pattern: melodramatic tone that robs the scene of comic irony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accumulation and cataloguing for comic weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Long lists of wages, prices, and contrasts (lieutenants one dollar, clerks four dollars, printers six and a half; gloves twelve dollars a dozen in Paris vs three or four here), and extended enumerations of social types in a procession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pile up concrete items, prices, or types to create rhythm and increasing absurdity or satire. Repetition and escalation amplify the comic point. Avoid excessively long lists with no punctuation or variation that tire the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understatement amid danger (litotes)
rubrics_metrics.description: "No fire was visible any where, but gusts of sulphurous steam issued silently and invisibly... But so long as we kept our nostrils buried in our handkerchiefs, there was small danger of suffocation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use understatement to minimize risk or horror in a way that produces ironic humor. The contrast between description and casual mitigation is comic. Anti-pattern: understatement so extreme it becomes confusing rather than funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification and grand metaphor to lampoon
rubrics_metrics.description: "With what majesty the monarch held his lonely state above the level sea!... His torch was out; his fires were smoldering; a tall column of smoke... was all the sign he gave that he was a living Autocrat of the Sea and not the spectre of a dead one."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give natural features regal or political personae to create lofty, mock‑epic descriptions that can be gently ridiculed by the surrounding comic commentary. Use elevated diction then undercut it. Anti-pattern: sustained grandiosity without a comic counterpoint.
